III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01325

The expression refers to his conjunction with the Moon’s inward reality: the Angel Gabriel, the Holy Spirit, who is identified with the Active Intelligence, the Angel of the Moon’s heaven and the Angel of Knowledge. The Prophet thereby inaugurates a time that can no longer be measured by the movements of the astronomical heavens. It belongs instead to their hidden reality, to heavens invisible to the bodily eye.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01326
There is, of course, a great difference between the Peripatetics presented here and those we ordinarily encounter in histories of philosophy.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01327

We must never lose sight of that difference. Here, the theory of knowledge is governed by the figure and function of the Active Intelligence as the Angel of Knowledge. It is directed toward an inner level of reality, where its task is to provide the foundation for a prophetic kind of philosophy. The passage from the Dabestân that we shall examine below will show how far the implications of this understanding could be carried. Such a theory of knowledge does not have to struggle toward an artificial reconciliation between faith and knowledge, official dogma and philosophical understanding.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01328

Instead, it makes possible both the experience and the philosophical grounding of one and the same supreme, profoundly personal encounter, appearing in two forms: that of the hero of prophecy and that of the hero of knowledge. Without some intuition of their underlying identity, no one could have recognized that the Angel of Revelation and the Active Intelligence are one and the same. And without that identity, the hidden meaning of the verse would remain unintelligible: “The Hour drew near, and the Moon split apart.”
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
en-book-4-ch-3-s5
5. The Theosophers of Light (Ishrâqiyûn)
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01329

The preceding discussion has already brought us close to the method followed by a fourth family of spiritual seekers: the Ishrâqiyûn, the theosophers of Light who follow Suhrawardî, in their search for the hidden meaning. At least in theory, we could distinguish their method from that of the Avicennian Peripatetics by recalling the distinction drawn in the introduction to Suhrawardî’s Hikmat al-Ishrâq. There, the Peripatetic sages are presented as outstanding philosophers who lack mystical experience, while the “Eastern sages”—above all, the sages of ancient Persia—are equally accomplished in philosophical reasoning and direct mystical experience.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01330

As we saw in Book II, Suhrawardî called these ancient Persian sages the Khosrawâniyûn, the spiritual ancestors of the Ishrâqiyûn. In practice, however, the philosophy of Light established by Suhrawardî, with its deliberate aim of reviving the teachings of ancient Iran, so quickly overshadowed the pure Avicennism from which his metaphysics had begun that we can speak, to a considerable extent, of an Ishrâqî form of Avicennism in Iran. The philosophers discussed in the preceding group already bear witness to this in their own way.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01331

As Sa’inoddin observes, the Avicennians and the Ishrâqiyûn begin by responding in the same way to the mysterious Quranic verse. According to celestial physics, the Moon belongs to a sphere composed of incorruptible matter and therefore cannot conceivably be split or torn apart. The verse cannot, then, be understood in terms of a physical phenomenon. Its real meaning must lie elsewhere.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01332

Having established this, the specifically Ishrâqî interpreter brings in the principles of the metaphysics of Light. The Avicennians had already affirmed and described a passage from the Moon’s outward reality to its inward reality. Their interpretation of the text already presupposed an event taking place within the interpreter’s own soul. It is this event that the Ishrâqiyûn now undertake to examine, drawing upon principles that connect their teaching with Gnosis and Manichaeism.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01333

To solve the riddle of the verse, they begin by recalling that Light is the very source of the world’s appearance (Persian: paydâ’i-e ’âlam). It is what makes it possible for anything to be manifest, revealed, or brought into view (paydâ, zâhir). Light is therefore the origin of everything that exists; indeed, light is identified with being itself.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01334

Yet their understanding of beings of light distinguishes two categories. There is a Light that cannot, in any way or in any sense, become mixed with Darkness. And there is a Light that can enter into such a mixture. The first category consists of the angelic Intelligences.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01335
The second consists of the celestial Souls, which move the heavenly spheres, and human souls, which have been entrusted with the task of governing material bodies.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01336

The first category possesses complete and actual knowledge of realities separated from matter—that is, the archetypal Ideas—without needing to pass through the experience of particular things. Souls belonging to the second category, however, can come to know both the pure Ideas and concrete realities accessible to the senses. The light of their being shines in both directions.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01337

Furthermore, if the entire order of beings is to reach completion and realize the fullest possible degree of perfection, every possible form of knowledge must become manifest: knowledge of pure Ideas no less than knowledge of concrete things. Nothing must remain merely potential. It is precisely this necessity that gives beings of light of the second category their particular task, and that determines their descent into matter and their temporary captivity within it. The Moon symbolizes these beings of light as they pass through a period of darkness and confinement.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01338

This mixture with Darkness is the condition that makes it possible for all the forms of knowledge—all the lights—previously held in a merely potential state to become fully manifest. Light, by its very nature, is both visible and revealed to itself and through itself (zâhir li-nafsi-hi), and that which reveals everything other than itself (mozhir li-ghayri-hi). Its power to bring things into appearance is inseparable from what it is.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01339

The rays it sends out return to it as reflections, multiplying without limit. In this way, Light eventually reaches the perfection of both its own manifestation (paydâ’î) and its power to reveal (paydâkunandagî). All the forms of knowledge, all the lights hidden within it in a state of potentiality, burst outward into manifestation.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01340

The darkened Moon at the beginning of its cycle becomes the full Moon blazing in the night sky. This is the splitting to which the Quranic verse alludes: the soul’s triumphant emergence from the Darkness in which it was held captive, because it has filled that very Darkness with its own Light.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01341

Yet for the soul to shine in Darkness in this way, the light hidden within it must first break forth. That emergence is the light of dawn: the soul’s knowledge rising into awareness. It is the soul’s own East, the place where its light rises—hence the expression “Eastern theosophy.” The soul’s state of manifestation reaches perfection because its power to reveal has reached its fullness. All the forms of knowledge contained within it have broken through the enclosure that held them captive and become manifest to the beings of every universe. This is why Light had to spend a time imprisoned in Darkness.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01342

Here the interpretation converges once more with that of the Avicennians. The “splitting of the Moon,” whose meaning is now becoming clear, is indeed the Sign of the approaching Hour, because the two expressions refer to one and the same event. The literalists could not see their unity because they were unable to recognize the depth of reality at which the event takes place.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01343

The Return, the Resurrection, the approaching Hour—these do not concern the scattered particles of an annihilated material body coming together again to reconstitute an individual who, in any case, could not be numerically identical to the original. They concern the Spirit, the eternally living being (zenda-ye jâvid), whose identity persists through every existence. This Spirit is the Light whose particular level of being required it to be joined for a time with the Darkness of the earthly body. Having completed its growth—as light itself can grow, as though there were a body composed entirely of light—it returns to its own world. That return is its resurrection.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01344

The Ishrâqiyûn pay close attention to this growth of a being of light (see Book II, Chapter V, on the meaning of the Moon’s phases in the Tale of the Crimson Archangel). Whenever Light encounters an opaque object that it cannot penetrate or pass through, the object casts a shadow. The light is turned back upon itself, as though reflected by a mirror, and its brightness increases through that reflection.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01345

In the same way, the living Light we call spirit, or the thinking soul, receives back the light that it projects, and grows accordingly. Certainly, what returns to the soul is its own light. What it perceives is the light reflected back to it by the screen—the body, the barzakh, or intermediate barrier—that intercepted it. The forms of knowledge that return to the soul are its own; the Image it projects upon things is its own Image.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01346
But it must project them outward in this way, so that it may see itself in a mirror. That mirror reveals the soul to itself and increases its light by reflecting back what it has received.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01347

For this to become possible, the soul had to descend into Darkness. Before its earthly existence, it was capable only of a comprehensive, undifferentiated kind of knowledge: knowledge of metaphysical universals. Once joined to a body, it became capable of grasping individual, concrete realities. To grasp them, to understand them, is to become conscious that the soul itself contains them, that they are present within it. This is how the complete manifestation of beings is achieved. When the soul reaches this perfection, not a single being in the upper world or the lower world remains absent from this being of light.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01348

The approaching Hour, of which the splitting of the Moon is the Sign, is therefore “the day when all secrets shall be revealed,” as another Quranic verse declares (86:9). But the meaning of this revelation is made clear by the Persian poet’s lines quoted by Sa’inoddin:
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01349
“Everything that has been, everything that is, everything that will be—understand that it all exists within yourself.”
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01350

At this degree, the movement inward is complete. The future and the past are no longer separate quantities of time scattered along the continuous extension of the world’s time, the time “of the horizons.” They are brought together into a single unity within the intensity of the “time of the soul.” At this degree, the entire chain of beings reaches its limit and perfection. It is the degree of the final Seal: both the state of manifestation and the power to reveal attain their fullness.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01351
The splitting of the Moon thus signifies the attainment of the degree of the Seal. But who possesses this final Seal? Historically, within the “time of the horizons,” it is certainly the Prophet.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01352

Yet according to the Ishrâqiyûn, the inner meaning of the verse becomes a reality in every spiritual seeker who reaches this degree. The conviction that the Prophet’s experience is the model for mystical experience is both the starting point and the outcome of an interpretation that takes the movement inward to its furthest depths. As we shall see, Semnânî carried it to the very limit.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01353

Through this inward transformation, philosophical wisdom becomes, in lived experience, a prophetic philosophy. Correspondingly, the religion of Islam itself is transformed into a purely spiritual Islam. Its philosophy is this prophetic philosophy, leading toward a transcendent realization of individual personhood through conjunction with the Angel of the supreme Revelation—the approaching Hour. Why, then, is the daring passage that bestows the title “Seal of Prophecy” upon every spiritual seeker missing from our manuscript of Sa’inoddin’s treatise? We shall encounter it later, in the context of the Dabestân, where it will provide the conclusion to our discussion.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
en-book-4-ch-3-s6
6. The Sufis
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01354

Sa’inoddin now presents three further ways of bringing meaning inward, corresponding to three spiritual families whose affinities may be more significant than their differences. We have deliberately spoken of different ways of going inward rather than of new depths to be reached. The interpretation developed by the Ishrâqiyûn already descends so deeply into the inner meaning of the Quranic verse that it would seem difficult to go further. What we encounter now are variations in the figures that become visible at a comparable depth of inward experience. Since these families of spiritual seekers are closely related, the figures that appear to their different forms of consciousness can be understood as corresponding to one another.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01355

In the two spiritual worlds we have just visited—that of the Neoplatonically inclined Peripatetics and that of the Ishrâqiyûn, the theosophers of Light—it was natural for the dominant figure to be the Active Intelligence. This Intelligence is identified with Gabriel, the Angel of Revelation, who among the Ishrâqiyûn is also identified with the archetypal Angel of humanity.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01356

If we keep in mind this identity between the Angel Gabriel and the heavenly Anthropos, the archetypal Human Being—an identity also found among the Mandaeans and the Ahl-e Haqq—we can recognize the corresponding figures that emerge at the horizon of consciousness beyond ordinary awareness. Sa’inoddin will now examine how these figures appear to the remaining three spiritual groups as they confront the same Quranic verse.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01357

The sixth group in Sa’inoddin’s overall classification consists of the Sufis. They are no longer divided, as they were in the earlier anonymous treatise, into pious ascetics, Sufis in general, and the faithful of love. The Sufis discussed here possess a sophisticated spiritual and philosophical culture. They are deeply shaped by the spirituality of both Suhrawardî and Ibn ’Arabî.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01358

Two terms describe them. First, they are Mohaqqiqûn: people who have personally verified the truth, both through philosophical reflection and through direct experience. They are, in the fullest sense, “those who have understood.”
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01359

This brings us back to the precise meaning we have given to the word hermeneutics: understanding is an act in which a person becomes conscious of what he himself contains and of the fact that he contains it. These Sufis are therefore also “speculative” thinkers in the original sense of the word. The speculative thinker becomes aware that he himself is the speculum, the mirror in which he sees all things, and that the Image appearing in this mirror is the image formed by his own understanding of them. The act of Understanding is thus inseparable from a personal realization.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01360

This explains their second designation: Ahl-e shohûd, those who have witnessed directly, initiates admitted to the contemplation of the mystery. Perhaps the closest equivalent is a Greek word drawn from the ancient language of the mysteries: they are epoptes, initiates who have been admitted to direct vision. We should also recall that, since the thirteenth century, the philosophy of Light shared in Iran by Suhrawardî’s Ishrâqiyûn and the disciples of Ibn ’Arabî has dominated philosophical mysticism. The Sufis now under discussion and the theosophers of Light previously described share several fundamental themes. The transition from one group to the other is therefore scarcely noticeable.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01361
We encounter here once again the idea of manifestation, understood in two related senses. First, there is the state of a being insofar as it is Light (Arabic zohûr, Persian paydâ’î).
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01362

Second, there is the power of manifestation—the power to reveal (Arabic izhâr, Persian paydâkunandagî)—that belongs to Light by virtue of its very being. Light illuminates from the instant it exists. It does not first come into existence and only afterward begin to shine. As soon as there exists something whose nature is to reveal, to bring something into view, there is already something revealed, something manifest—a “phenomenon” (zâhir).
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01363

Here, however, the question is no longer the destiny of the individual soul as a being of Light: the necessary drama of its descent into Darkness and its redemption. It is the fact of theophany in general—the appearance or manifestation of the divine—insofar as theophany is bound up with the Human Form. In a sense, we are now considering the prologue to the drama contemplated by the Ishrâqiyûn.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01364

It is from this standpoint that the idea of theophany provides a solution to the riddle of the Quranic verse chosen by Sa’inoddin for his treatise. He begins with a brief reference to a hadîth familiar throughout Islamic theosophy, and especially fundamental to the teaching of Ibn ’Arabî:
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01365
“I was a Hidden Treasure, and I loved to be known. So I created creatures in order that I might be known.”
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01366

As Sa’inoddin reminds us, the whole of philosophical Sufism rests upon the idea that the “descents” (tanazzolât) of the primordial Source of being (asl-e wojûd)—from the levels of the Pleroma, the fullness of the higher spiritual world, down to creatures subject to becoming—have one ultimate purpose. The Source emerges in forms of infinite multiplicity so that it may reveal and manifest itself.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01367

There are two degrees corresponding to two aspects of this manifestation. The first is the resulting state of manifestation (martaba-ye zohûr o paydâ’î): the degree at which everything possible passes into actual, manifest existence. The fullness of this theophany is the “Human Form,” which the Sufis express through the personal symbol of Adam. In doing so, they too give expression to the Gnostic idea of the heavenly Anthropos, the archetypal Human Being. This essence is perfect because it brings together every degree of being. It gathers all existence into itself, because in it and through it the whole of being attains the level of a form conscious of itself.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01368

In its second aspect—the second degree of its perfection—this manifestation is considered no longer simply as the state brought about by the divine will to reveal itself, but as an active function inherent in that state. What has been revealed now itself reveals what is manifested within it. In this sense, the recipient of an action becomes its agent; what is revealed becomes what reveals.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01369
Yet the two movements—acting and receiving—take place simultaneously and reciprocally.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01370

Through the divine will to manifest itself, the Godhead reveals the Human Form by revealing itself within that Form. At the same moment, the Human Form reveals the Godhead precisely because the Godhead reveals the Form. Perfect theophany is a divine “anthropomorphosis,” a manifestation in human form. The Human Form assumes the highest power of revealing the divine. By serving as the bearer of the divine Attributes, it allows the Godhead in its own essence to remain free of every suggestion of “anthropomorphism,” or limitation to human shape.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01371

In the philosophical terminology of Sufism, the Seal (khâtim) designates the person whose state of human perfection invests him, in the highest degree, with this power of divine manifestation. That investiture is the bursting into view of an inner meaning previously hidden beneath the perfected form. It is the manifestation, through that form, of the Forma Dei, the Form of God. This does not mean that the person incarnates the divine Form in the technical Christian sense of incarnation. Rather, he bears it within himself as a mirror bears an image. (We can recognize here the displacement of a Shiite doctrine of the Imams, an imamology that no longer speaks its own name.)
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01372

As in the symbolism of the Ishrâqiyûn, the Moon represents this perfected Form. The splitting of the Moon mentioned in the Quranic verse is the Hour of theophany: the moment when the divine becomes manifest in the mirror of the perfected Form, when the Human Form takes on the likeness of the divine. The initiated contemplative, the epoptes, beholds this directly, without needing to construct an argument or proceed through philosophical reasoning.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01373

At once, the connection between the two parts of the Quranic verse becomes clear in a flash. Everything, every being, returns to its origin. For the Human Form, the return to its origin—the approaching Hour, the Resurrection—is the moment when it fully assumes its power to reveal the divine. It has become a pure, untarnished mirror, and the Forma Dei appears within it as an image appears in a mirror.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01374

Now, the Perfect Human Being is the one in whom and through whom everything that was merely potential has become manifest. As a microcosm, this person thus performs the work of divine self-revelation. According to the Sufis discussed by Sa’inoddin, such a spiritual being is designated by the term nabî: prophet. (We shall see, in Semnânî’s teaching, the degree of inward realization corresponding to the birth of the nabî as an inner spiritual state.) Among the Avicennian philosophers and the Ishrâqiyûn, the philosopher’s vocation was already directed toward a “prophetic philosophy,” bringing him into relation with the prophet’s experience and calling. In the same way, the Sufi mystic is directed toward the archetype of the nabî.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01375

At this point, the oppositions that our accustomed rational categories have taught us to make lose their force: philosophy itself is prophetic, mystical experience is a prophetic state, and the reverse is equally true. Spiritual life is centered entirely on the figure of the nabî, the prophet (just as Christian spiritual life is centered on Christology). Consequently, the very idea of the Seal is transformed by the mysterious event to which the Qur'anic verse alludes. The title borne on earth by the one who was the “Seal of the Prophets” is transferred to every spiritual seeker who, in turn, attains the state of nabî. For the state and calling of the nabî belong to the person to whom, and through whom, the Forma Dei, the divine Form, is revealed.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01376

We shall soon see that this is the profound conviction of the Ishrâqiyûn, the philosophers of illumination. Both they and the Sufis whom Sâ'inoddîn has in mind express through this shared conception their belief that the prophetic gift continues.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01377

But this brings us back to a serious question we have already encountered: what unspoken assumptions are these two groups making? Let us review the matter. We have just read that, for the Ishrâqiyûn and for the Sufis Sâ'inoddîn is discussing, every spiritual seeker reaches full inner perfection by attaining the state of nabî. The prophet thus remains the archetype that spiritual life seeks to realize. This is of the greatest interest, but some distinctions are essential. To begin with, there can be no question of repeating the role of the lawgiving prophet or the prophet sent on a mission. Only the state of the nabî in the simplest sense can serve as the model.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01378

Yet to make this distinction is already to invoke the categories established by Shiite teachings on prophecy (see Book I, Chapter VI). Those teachings also tell us that, after the man who was the “Seal of the Prophets” in the absolute sense, the term nabî can no longer be used. Instead, for the period following Muhammad, the word is walî—a friend or beloved of God. In terms of the inner states experienced, the walî corresponds to what the simple term nabî designated throughout the pre-Muhammadan era.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01379

So when we are told that the mystic's experience follows the model of the prophet's, this cannot possibly refer to the lawgiving mission of the Messenger invested with nobowwat al-tashrî', the authority to reveal a religious law. It can refer only to what, in the prophet-messenger himself, is the source of his prophetic status (nobowwat) and of his outward mission to others: his walâyat, his intimate spiritual nearness to God.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01380

Are we therefore facing, in the Sufis described by Sâ'inoddîn, precisely the paradox denounced by Haydar Âmolî? Is this a Sufism that has forgotten its origins, one from which Shiite imamology has effectively been made to disappear, even though it is presupposed by the very notion of a distinctive prophetic gift continuing after the last prophet and the closing of the prophetic cycle? Or is this an instance of taqîyeh, esoteric discretion, deliberately concealing every sign of an openly acknowledged Shiism? Sâ'inoddîn gives us at least the beginnings of an answer in his final paragraph, where he places the spiritual schools he has described in relation to Shiism.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01381

In comparison with Shiism, all of them have thus far been no more than the approaching Hour—or, more precisely, signs that the Hour is approaching. The “splitting of the Moon” does not take place—that is, its spiritual meaning cannot be perceived—unless one has learned from the “Pillars of the Prophet's House,” a reference to the line of the Twelve Imams.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01382

Unfortunately, this final paragraph is deliberately brief and allusive (see §8 below). But perhaps we can make progress by studying the pages apparently lost from Sâ'inoddîn's text, which we have recovered in the Dabestân: the pages concerning the Avicennian philosophers and the Ishrâqiyûn.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01383

We can then compare them with what we already know of Shiite spirituality founded on walâyat—what we have called its orientation around the Imam. Perhaps this will allow us to place the earlier degrees of esoteric understanding in relation to Shiism as the “seventh degree,” and to understand why Sâ'inoddîn regards all those earlier degrees as merely the “approach of the Hour.” The outlines of Sâ'inoddîn Torkeh's religious typology would then become clearer, helping us understand the spirituality of Iranian Islam as a whole. Before that, however, the author identifies one further spiritual group. It occupies the last stage before Shiite imamology, which is at once the source of all hidden meanings and the summit toward which they rise.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
en-book-4-ch-3-s7
7. The Hurufis
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01384

This name designates those who practice the “science of letters” ('ilm-e horûf). In Islam, they carry forward a tradition dating to the beginnings of Ismaili Shiism in the eighth century. The techniques of their science correspond, even in their details, to those practiced by Kabbalists, although the science of letters is only one part of the immense spiritual tradition known as Kabbalah. By training the initiate to see each letter as a symbol or an ideogram encoding a value, this science makes possible an immediate, intuitive perception that no longer needs the assistance of intellectual argument. It, too, is directed toward the prophetic model. As Sâ'inoddîn tells us: “Their contemplation proceeds through the same Forms that descended upon the prophets.”
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01385

The later religious community known in Iran by this name, for whom the science of letters was the defining doctrine, originated with a man whose fate was tragic: Fazlollah, a northern Iranian from Astarâbâd, executed as a martyr in 796 AH (1393–94 CE) on the orders of Mîrânshâh, one of Tamerlane's sons. The emergence of his teaching and his tragic death mark an important stage in the history of Iranian Shiism.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01386

The Hurufis' interpretation of the Qur'anic verse about the splitting of the Moon presupposes their entire metaphysics, because that metaphysics concentrates on the very phenomenon that most urgently calls for a conscious art of interpretation. It is not concerned with conceptual dialectic. Its essential concern is to interpret the Word: the spoken Word, in the form of sounding incantation, and the Word fixed—or, more precisely, symbolized—in writing. From this emerges the outline of an ontology of writing, an understanding of being through written forms. The shapes of letters are grasped intuitively as ideograms, since every stroke of the design can itself carry an ideographic value. Sâ'inoddîn, who died some thirty-five years after the movement's founder, knew the doctrine at first hand. He sketches it in a way we can summarize here, emphasizing a few of its characteristic features.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01387

Being exists at many levels. The beings found on these levels differ in their capacity for existence and their receptivity to it. Because those capacities differ, we must first distinguish beings that can subsist in themselves and possess an independent existence: the Spirits at the various levels of their hierarchy, and bodies, whether heavenly, subtle, or material. Other beings cannot subsist independently. They exist only through something else—through the subject whose state or activity they are. Examples include actions, events, and words.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01388

Now, among the very sources (ommohât) of the levels of being, one holds a privileged position: the Word (Kalâm). Everything that can exist in the divine worlds or in the worlds of becoming—and even everything that has been unable to achieve existence in either the world of universals or that of concrete individual things—can come into existence at this privileged level of the Word. There is more. One of its distinctive powers is that it makes manifest the meanings and significance of all actual and possible beings. Ideas, doctrines, theories, realities of every kind: they become manifest, enter the light, and acquire the status of meaningful “phenomena” only by reaching the level of the Word.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01389

Yet the Word is not itself an autonomous level of being, subsisting on its own. The fullness of revelation that it confers on things by “uttering” them is borrowed from the one who utters it—the motakallim. Its existence depends on the existence of that speaker.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01390

This brief account by Sâ'inoddîn brings into focus the guiding conviction of these Islamic Kabbalists. For them, interpretation—the passage from outward appearance to hidden meaning—is, in both the etymological and the deepest sense, an onto-logy: an understanding of being through the Word. For at the innermost depth of things, being itself is a Word, a Logos. That is why they say, for example, that sound does not originate outside the objects that strike one another.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01391

Rather, it emerges from within them, from their hidden, inward reality. The distinction between outward and inward meaning, on which the spiritual interpretation considered here depends, is also the condition of every being and every thing. The inward (bâtin)—what is hidden, unseen, unheard, and inaccessible to the senses—is each being's absolute essence (dhât motlaq), its energy from before eternity, its eternal and unchanging King, its constitutive Word.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01392

Yet beings and things do not make that Word audible unless there is a collision. Until then, its sound remains a latent possibility buried within them. As long as the two things do not strike each other, the divine Word (Kalâm-e Haqq) remains submerged and entombed in them. The deepest secret of a being is thus understood as the sounding incantation that calls it into existence, a secret revealed only through that impact. Its sound is the manifestation of its innermost depth, its own distinctive rate of vibration.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01393

To know a being, then, is to discern beneath its outward manifestation (zâhir) the hidden reality (bâtin) of the divine Word that uttered it and that it itself utters. This Word does not exist independently outside the being, for it is the being's very existence. The Word becomes manifest only through the manifestation of the one who speaks it, just as moonlight is nothing other than a revelation of the Sun's light. In a sense, the Sun “utters” that light; without it, the Moon would remain in the darkness of nonbeing. That is why, Sâ'inoddîn observes, the Moon can symbolize the level of being under discussion. Here we already glimpse the mystical meaning that will be found in the Qur'anic verse about the Moon's splitting: the bursting forth of the Word, a triumphant sounding incantation.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01394

Unfortunately, sound is unstable and short-lived. Yet it can take a form more substantial and lasting than a momentary vibration, a form that is itself privileged because it reveals the effects, traces, and laws of being more clearly than any other. That form is the pattern traced by writing. On the one hand, the Word exists only through the one who utters it. On the other, this subtle and fragile mode of existence—existence as sound, the vibration produced by the impact that draws from beings the secret incantation of their existence—acquires a stable, lasting form in written signs, always ready to be awakened again into incantation.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01395

Hence the fundamental importance of writing, whose reach is as universal as that of the Word itself. If the inward reality of a being is its secret Word, then its outward appearance, its visible features, become writing that conceals a secret, a code. Every being becomes an ideogram. Above all, the human face becomes an ideogram—or sacred inscription—of invisible divine beauty. The Divine Being is the Word immanent in every being. The Hurufi idea of creation, like Ibn 'Arabî's, does not involve some extra-divine existence being added to the being of the divine Creator.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01396

The eternal Word becomes actual by taking on determinate, particular forms: it gives birth to the written letters. These are the twenty-eight letters of the Arabic alphabet (or twenty-nine if lâm-alef is counted), with which the Qur'an is written and which constitute the “Muhammadan Word” (Kalima mohammadiya); or the thirty-two letters of the Persian alphabet, which constitute the “Adamic Word” (Kalima âdamiya).
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01397

Letters here play a role analogous to the latent archetypes of beings, their eternally established individual realities (a'yân thâbita) in Ibn 'Arabî's thought. Everything we can imagine or conceive is expressed through the twenty-eight or thirty-two letters, corresponding to as many divine attributes. The sound, the audible Word encoded by the letters and spoken through them, is the divine Essence itself. That Essence is neither substance nor accident; it reveals itself through this sounding incantation. We have here a remarkable first outline of a phenomenology of music.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01398

Hence the extraordinary complexity and precise rules governing the different ways of reading letters: simple numerical calculation, analysis of the letters composing a word, rules of permutation, and so on. All these techniques are known in Kabbalah, and among the Hurufis they continue the practices of the Ismailis. As Sâ'inoddîn observes, such techniques allow an intuitive apprehension of the very Forms that descended on the prophets from the most holy Heaven, without constructing logical arguments or passing through the philosophers' conceptual dialectic.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01399

Writing is thus as universal a phenomenon as the Word; its visible design fixes the sounding incantation in a lasting, encoded form. If one can hear the secret Word of each being, and hear each being as a Word, one must also be able to decipher its outward appearance as an ideogram—as the code of its own distinctive Word.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01400

Hurufi interpretation, as an ontology in which being is Word, therefore also requires a science of the visible forms of beings, above all the study of the human face. Hurufi authors speak of the human being as a “Qur'an in human form.” As a microcosm, the human being is even the archetype of the holy Book, the “Mother of the Book” (omm al-Kitâb). A human face can be read like a Qur'an; the principles of spiritual interpretation, or ta'wîl, can be applied to it.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01401

The beauty of a perfect human face then reveals the secret of theophany, the manifestation of God. This devotion to human beauty and to the beautiful face, already found in Iranian Sufism before the Hurufis, reaches among them an ecstatic worship of beauty (see above, Book III, on Rûzbehân's Sufism). What the initiate experiences before beauty has nothing to do with a frivolous, possessive, or merely worldly feeling. It belongs to the realm of the sacred and overwhelming. It brings exaltation and despair together, perhaps joy and terror as well. For to reach what beauty reveals, one would have to pass “through the other side of the mirror.”
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01402

The correspondences are carried very far, sometimes with a degree of artificiality. What matters is the result in which these mystics delight. The surah that opens the Qur'an, the Fâtiha, has seven verses—seven âyât, a word whose original sense is “signs.” The human face likewise bears seven lines or “seven signs.” Through these correspondences, the features and meaning of its beauty can be related to the meaning of Revelation, allowing the face of a beautiful person to be contemplated as the face of God.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01403

The seven lines are the four lines of the eyelashes, the two lines of the eyebrows, and the line formed by the hair. They are the “maternal lines” (khotût ommîya), or “lines of Eve,” as opposed to the “paternal lines” that appear on a man's face only after puberty, where the beard begins to grow. The feminine lines are therefore the most essential, since they appear in every human being—in women and in men before adulthood. And it was under precisely these features, these feminine lines and seven divine inscriptions, that God showed his face to the Prophet in a vision on which the Sufis have meditated without end.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01404

For these mystics, the beauty of a face and the rapture it inspires were the highest manifestation of the divine in this world. It was in this sense that they spoke of the “paradise of the face” (jannat-e didâr). A Persian poem by 'Alî al-A'lâ, inspired by something very close to Rûzbehân's vision, goes so far as to ask: “Why, at the sight of beautiful faces, are you struck with bewilderment, intoxication, and madness? If these faces are not themselves the visible form of the divine … why do you let yourself die at the feet of the beauties you adore?”
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01405

Beauty is the secret of God's will to reveal himself: the will that human beings should behold him. And what God reveals—the form through which they can begin to sense him—is human beauty as Forma Dei, the form of God (sûrat al-Haqq). From prophet to prophet, through the 124,000 nabîs spoken of in tradition, down to the ill-fated Fazlollah, the same Form has sought to disclose its mystery to humanity, only to be rejected, reviled, stoned, and crucified. Abraham sought the “signs” of divinity among the stars until he discovered them upon his own face. He read “his own Book”; then he broke every idol and bowed before the absolute Essence. So it was with Moses and with Muhammad.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01406

In short, there is a “silent Qur'an” (Qorân sâmit) and a “speaking Qur'an” (Qorân nâtiq). The speaking Qur'an is the human face, the Word made manifest. To read the true Qur'an, to decipher its hidden meaning completely, is to understand the essential “seven signs” revealed by the human-and-divine face.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01407

But we must attend to a crucial point: in Shiite gnosis, the “Silent One” is a technical designation for the Imam, complementing the “Enunciator” (Nâtiq, the “Speaking One”), who is the prophet. As a theophany, beauty thus performs a prophetic function. The hidden meaning to which it points, like every spoken Word, is therefore the invisible Imam, in his state of heavenly humanity.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01408

This brief recollection of the Hurufi system is enough to place their interpretation of the Qur'anic verse about the splitting of the Moon among those of the related spiritual schools, and to understand how they turn its meaning inward. For them, too, the verse plainly does not describe an event in the visible heavens studied by astronomy. Its spiritual meaning emerges on two levels at once: the visual and the audible.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01409

Consider first what the Moon symbolizes. Left to itself, it remains dark. The light of the Sun rises within it and gradually brings it to incandescence, until, gazing at itself reflected in itself, it may cry out, “I am the Sun.”
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01410

But the darkened Moon also symbolizes the original silence of a written line, an ideogram not yet deciphered. From that silence the Word is uttered, and suddenly its primordial, original meaning “bursts forth.” What bursts forth is the hidden being itself, the meaning of the existence within whose secret the Word had lain submerged—silent, not yet able to “speak itself.” Or again: from the face of beauty that has been misunderstood, profaned, and degraded, the overwhelming meaning of Beauty bursts forth as a divine manifestation. It fascinates and torments us with an unappeased longing: a longing like the expectation of an apotheosis that would lift the veil from the mystery momentarily glimpsed in the fleeting light of a beautiful face.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01411

The Ishrâqiyûn and the Sufis have already helped us understand the “sign of the approaching Hour” in this way: Light breaks through the enclosing darkness, attains its perfect manifestation, and fully realizes its power to reveal. The masters of the science of letters are reflecting upon the same teaching: everything returns to its origin. The Form that makes this return is the primordial heavenly Form that existed before the stain of darkness and its mixture with material bodies. It is the divine Word taking a particular mode in the incantation uttered by each being; it is the perfect Form of the “twenty-nine letters” that descends in its fullness from prophet to prophet until it reaches the “Seal of the Prophets.”
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01412

From then on it can be perceived in the written signs of the Book—a code mute and unreadable to the uninitiated and the unawakened. This Book is both the holy volume whose pages bear written signs and the beautiful face marked with those same divine inscriptions. Whenever the meaning of the letters and signs emerges and shines through, the pure, primordial Word resounds. The Book—“your own Book,” as in Abraham's case—becomes, in the fullest sense, the “Speaking One” that reveals the Silent One. This is the signal of resurrection and return, and this is the meaning of the verse: “The Hour drew near, and the Moon split.”
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
en-book-4-ch-3-s8
8. The Shiites
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01413

However deeply we have now entered the esoteric meaning of this verse, Sâ'inoddîn still reserves for us a final stage: a seventh spiritual group, “those endowed with strength and vision” (Qur'an 38:45). They are the Prophet's closest intimates, the heirs to his perfection. Brief as the indications are, they allow us to place the meaning that crowns all the others, the meaning properly disclosed by Shiite spiritual interpretation.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01414

What is of exceptional interest here is that, for our author, the Shiite reading of the verse gathers together all the esoteric meanings previously examined. Each of them presupposes that reading because it brings their truth to completion.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01415

We must therefore say: philosophy in its true sense, the theosophy of Light in its true sense, Sufism in its true sense—all of these are Shiism. The fundamental Shiite idea is that of theophany (zohûr, mazhar), the manifestation of God in the persons of the holy Imams. The ideas of the Ishrâqiyûn, the Sufis, and the Hurufis are therefore the “approaching Hour” of this central idea.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01416

What these schools share is the thought of God taking human form on the plane of an angelic, more-than-human existence. It runs from Gabriel, the angelic archetype of humanity for the Ishrâqiyûn, to the human form whose ideal beauty reveals the Forma Dei. Throughout, the Shiite idea remains present as an intimation: the Imam, in his perfect heavenly humanity, is the mirror (mazhar), the eternal theophany in which human beings contemplate this divine Form, and to which the prophet's Word refers.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01417

Here again, the interpretation of the verse presupposes the “perfect Word” of the “Seal of Prophecy” (Kalâm-e kâmil-e khâtam al-nobowwa). This Word is called the “Perfection of the Form” (Kamâl-e sûrat). It conceals and contains the fullness of meaning, all spiritual meanings; within it is implied, brought to the highest perfection, the meaning of everything that was, is, and will be. Certainly, Sâ'inoddîn tells us, many spiritually perfected and realized people (Kâmilân o mohaqqiqân) have set out in the right direction to discover the true meaning of the Return (ma'âd). Many profound meanings have been unveiled to them in keeping with their capacity for mystical perception.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01418

Yet the fullness of meaning, the deepest significance of what is meant by the “Word,” has not become wholly transparent to them. For the key to spiritual meaning, the power to make meaning burst forth through this “perfect Form”—the divine assumption of form in the archetypal, heavenly humanity of the Imam—in short, the knowledge of ta'wîl in its fullness, must be learned from the “Pillars of the Prophet's Family” (Asâtîn-e Ahl-e Bayt), meaning the line of the Twelve Imams.
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)
passage-en-01419

Only then does the Qur'anic verse announcing the splitting of the Moon, and the event it signifies, “show the Way and give the signal, in a manner and in a sense well known to them and their followers. This short treatise cannot say more. Should an eager seeker taste a desire to know more of these mysteries, let him consult the longer treatises.”
III. A Typology of Spiritual Seekers According to Sa’inoddin ’Alî Torkeh Ispahânî (d. 830/1427)

9. An Imamology That Dares Not Speak Its Name
